title: Sallowgate's Empty Boxes
passage:
The bat boxes on the north gable of the Sallowgate laundry have been up for eleven years. Not one of them has ever held a bat. They are handsome objects, cast in a pale aggregate that matches the render and set flush with the wall, each with a rough landing strip beneath a slot two fingers wide, and they went up under a condition of the planning consent that turned the laundry into flats. Four streets away, on a school converted the same year, a row of boxes in the same position on the same kind of gable fills most summers. For a long time nobody at the borough could say what separated the two.

Emrys Talbourne has surveyed roosts for Drimmond council since the conversions began, and he spent three summers logging temperatures rather than counting animals. The colonies displaced by the work had mostly been living in roof voids – the shallow, dusty gap between the slates and the boarding beneath them, running the length of a ridge. A void of that kind is not one habitat but a shifting range of them. Slate heats quickly. By four in the afternoon the space near the ridge can stand at close to thirty degrees while the eaves end, shaded and open to the air, sits ten or twelve degrees below it, and by dawn the whole void has given its heat back. Talbourne's loggers show the animals working through that gradient: high and deep in the warm hours, when the young grow fastest, out towards the cooler eaves at night. "I would not say they are choosing a temperature," he told me. "I would say that where the choice is missing, they do not stay long."

Not everyone in the borough reads the record that way. Beatrix Oyelaran, Drimmond's building conservation officer, thinks the temperature account has been asked to carry more than it can. Her objection is documentary, and it is about timing. She went back through the consent files and found that most of the boxes that failed had been put up in June or July, when the local colonies were long settled for the season and had no reason to prospect for anywhere new. Among the earliest boxes, those fitted between September and February were taken up about three times as often as the summer ones. "You can hang the finest box in the county in the middle of July," she said, "and it will stand empty, and that will have nothing to do with what it is made of." On the early boxes she was plainly right, and Talbourne says so.

What he did next was hold the timing constant. Across two autumns twenty-four boxes went up on nine buildings, all fitted out of season and all logged: twelve cut from thick untreated timber, twelve cast in the same aggregate as the laundry's. The timber boxes moved about eleven degrees between afternoon and dawn, and nine of the twelve were occupied within two summers. The cast boxes held to three degrees or less, and two were used. Both of those two sat on a chimney breast whose flue still carried warm air up from the block's boiler, and the loggers inside them recorded a swing much like the timber's; cast boxes on two other south-facing walls, with nothing behind them but insulation, stayed empty. One of the three timber boxes that stayed empty hangs over a yard lit all night; Talbourne suspects the lighting and has not tested it. The school's row, he adds, is boarded timber, and it swings twelve degrees. Oyelaran accepts the second series and still holds that timing explains more of the whole record than he allows.

Drimmond's guidance was rewritten last winter. It names a material, caps the wall thickness of a box, and requires that new ones be fitted between September and the end of February, though the fire officer has asked for the timber clause to be looked at again. Nothing in it reaches the boxes already on walls, and nobody has proposed taking those down. The row on the laundry's north gable is still there, still flush, still pale against the render. No one has had a ladder up to it since March.
– Perrin Hadleigh

questions.prompt: What does the text say about the row of boxes on the converted school?

options.text: It has been occupied every single summer since the boxes first went up on that gable.
It was fitted in the autumn, while the row at the laundry went up in the middle of July.
Bats use it in most summers, although it sits in the same position as the laundry's row.
It was logged for three summers before the borough agreed to attach any condition to conversions.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 1, first local item in passage order. WHY-KEY (C): paragraph 1 states that 'Four streets away, on a school converted the same year, a row of boxes in the same position on the same kind of gable fills most summers.' C paraphrases both halves – the hedged occupancy ('in most summers') and the matched position – without lifting a distinctive run. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = quantifier_upgrade (the engineered dominant ELF trap) – absolutises the planted hedge 'fills most summers' into 'occupied every single summer'; tempting because a skimmer remembers only that the school's row works. B = outside_knowledge – imports a plausible explanation (autumn fitting versus a July fitting at the laundry) that the passage never states about either row; the June/July finding in paragraph 3 concerns 'most of the boxes that failed' across the borough, not this pair, and the text says 'For a long time nobody at the borough could say what separated the two'. D = wrong_location – the 'three summers' of logging belong to Talbourne's own survey work in paragraph 2 ('he spent three summers logging temperatures rather than counting animals'), not to the school's row, and no condition on conversions is said to follow from it.

questions.prompt: What are we told about the roof voids the displaced colonies had been using?

options.text: The animals kept to the shaded eaves in the hottest part of the day and moved up to the ridge at night.
Heat rising from the rooms below kept the space above the boarding warmer than the air outside at night.
The difference between the two ends was as wide at dawn as it had been in the late afternoon.
The animals were up at the warm end while the afternoon heat lasted, and out at the cool end after dark.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 2, local order. STEM-LAW: the stem names the voids but entails nothing about what they were like, so all four options are open on form. WORLD-KNOWLEDGE: the option set is built so that general knowledge cannot settle the item. That a roof void has a warm end and a cool end, and that the animals move between them, is ordinary roost ecology – so A and D BOTH assert it, and asserting it discriminates nothing. What decides the item is the DIRECTION of that movement across the day, which the passage states plainly and which everyday intuition gets backwards. WHY-KEY (D): paragraph 2 reports that by four in the afternoon 'the space near the ridge can stand at close to thirty degrees while the eaves end, shaded and open to the air, sits ten or twelve degrees below it', and that 'Talbourne's loggers show the animals working through that gradient: high and deep in the warm hours, when the young grow fastest, out towards the cooler eaves at night.' High and deep is the ridge end, which is the warm one at that hour; out towards the eaves is the cool one. D states exactly that, in different words. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = reversed_direction, the engineered dominant trap here – it runs the same movement the other way, shade while the day is hot and warmth once it is dark, which is what a reader who has not read the paragraph assumes an animal does; the text says the opposite and supplies the reason, that the young grow fastest in the warm hours. B = outside_knowledge – a genuinely plausible building-physics claim (warmth from the rooms below) that the passage never makes; the text attributes the heat to the roof covering ('Slate heats quickly') and reports the void cold again by morning. C = scope_shift over time – takes the ten-or-twelve-degree spread measured at four in the afternoon and holds it through to first light, which the same sentence denies: 'by dawn the whole void has given its heat back', so by then the two ends have converged.

questions.prompt: What does the passage suggest about the two cast boxes that were occupied?

options.text: The temperature range inside them was supplied by the warm flue behind, not by the boxes.
They were the only cast boxes in the trial that had been fitted on a south-facing wall.
Cast boxes work as well as timber ones provided they are hung high on a sunny wall.
Their aggregate had been mixed thinner than the laundry's, so it gave up its heat more quickly.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-002 (inference / implication), one logical inch beyond paragraph 4. WHY-KEY (A): paragraph 4 reports that 'The cast boxes held to three degrees or less, and two were used. Both of those two sat on a chimney breast whose flue still carried warm air up from the block's boiler, and the loggers inside them recorded a swing much like the timber's.' Cast material by itself held three degrees or less; these two swung like timber; and the one thing behind them that the cast boxes the passage documents as empty lacked was a live flue – those sat on two other south-facing walls, 'with nothing behind them but insulation'. (The passage reports the backing of only two of the other ten cast boxes, so the contrast is drawn against those two and not against all ten.) The inference is that the range was supplied by the building, not by the box – exactly what A says. WHY-DISTRACTORS: B = too_literal / contradicted – fastens on aspect rather than the flue, and the same sentence records 'cast boxes on two other south-facing walls, with nothing behind them but insulation, stayed empty', so these two were not the only south-facing cast boxes. C = too_far – a two-step leap into a general recommendation about how cast boxes should be hung; the passage reports two boxes on one heated breast, not a rule for sunny walls. D = outside_knowledge – invents a difference in the mix that the text never mentions; the passage says the trial boxes were 'cast in the same aggregate as the laundry's'.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's attitude to Oyelaran's objection?

options.text: Convinced: the writer agrees with her that what a box is made of hardly matters at all.
Sceptical: the writer grants the objection some force but thinks her file search far too small.
Accepting as far as it goes: right about the earliest boxes, but not about the later series.
Dismissive: the writer treats it as a procedural complaint that the temperature record has already answered.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-005 (stance / tone / attitude); the challenger here is partly right, so the item turns on how far the writer goes with her. HEDGE BALANCE: the four stance labels split two absolute (A 'Convinced', D 'Dismissive') against two qualified (B 'Sceptical', C 'Accepting as far as it goes'), and A's body is hedged as well ('hardly matters at all'), so picking the qualified option narrows the field to B and C but cannot choose between them – only the direction the writer actually takes decides it, and that is in the passage. WHY-KEY (C): the writer endorses the timing point in plain words – 'On the early boxes she was plainly right, and Talbourne says so' – but then reports the second series, in which 'What he did next was hold the timing constant' and all twenty-four boxes were 'fitted out of season', and lets the timber/cast split stand as a result the timing objection does not reach; Oyelaran's continuing claim that 'timing explains more of the whole record than he allows' is reported as her position, not endorsed. C names precisely that bounded acceptance. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = role_or_attribution_swap (the TYPE-005 signature) – hands the writer Oyelaran's own quoted claim that an empty box 'will have nothing to do with what it is made of'; tempting because hers is the most forceful line in the text, and A is softened ('hardly matters') so that it does not read as an obvious overstatement. B = polarity error in the qualified register – the writer never questions her file search and never calls the sample small; the text concedes the point outright. D = polarity overshoot – turns a granted objection into a complaint brushed aside, which 'she was plainly right' contradicts.

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: The conditions that planning authorities attach to the conversion of old buildings into housing.
Why some purpose-built replacement roosts are taken up by bats while others stand empty.
Talbourne's decision to give up counting animals altogether and record temperatures in their place.
A disagreement between two council officers over how much of a converted building should be kept.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-004 (main idea / whole-text focus), edge position 5. WHY-KEY (B): the passage opens on a matched pair – the laundry's boxes where 'Not one of them has ever held a bat' beside a school row that 'fills most summers' – states that 'For a long time nobody at the borough could say what separated the two', works through the void measurements, the timing objection and the twenty-four-box series, and ends with rewritten guidance and one row still empty. The question the whole text pursues is which replacement boxes get used and which do not; B states that without claiming the answer is settled. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = scope_error – planning conditions are the frame in which the boxes exist ('a condition of the planning consent that turned the laundry into flats') and the closing paragraph does report rewritten guidance, but the text argues nothing about planning practice in general. C = detail-as-main, distorted – Talbourne did spend 'three summers logging temperatures rather than counting animals', but 'give up counting animals altogether' overstates a method choice within one survey, and a method is not the text's subject. D = surface_word_match – Talbourne and Oyelaran do disagree, yet about why boxes fail, not about how much original fabric a conversion should keep; the phrase borrows her job title ('building conservation officer') for a dispute the text never stages.
